title: C++ Fundamentals Handbook: Types, Memory and Compilation
summary: Quick revision notes on C++ types, const, references vs pointers, parameter passing, arrays, stack vs heap, nullptr, overloading and the header/compilation model.

chapters.title: Types, Const and the Mental Model
points: C++ is statically typed: every variable has a fixed type at compile time; sizes are implementation-defined (int >= 16 bits, typically 32; long long >= 64; use <cstdint> int32_t, uint64_t when width matters)
Initialization: brace init int x{5}; rejects narrowing (int x{3.5} is an error) while int x = 3.5 silently truncates to 3; auto x = 5; deduces int and drops top-level const and references
const makes an object read-only after init and must be initialized: const int n = 10; constexpr additionally requires a compile-time value, so it can size arrays: constexpr int N = 8; int a[N];
Reading const with pointers: const int* p = pointer to const data (can't change *p); int* const p = const pointer (can't reseat p); const int* const p = both. Rule: read the declaration right to left

Mistake: integer overflow on signed int is undefined behavior, and mixing signed with unsigned (-1 < 1u is false) converts the signed value to unsigned; uninitialized locals hold garbage, so always initialize

chapters.title: References vs Pointers and Pass by Value
points: A reference int& r = x; is an alias for an existing object: must be initialized, can never be reseated, cannot be null, and uses no dereference syntax
A pointer int* p = &x; holds an address: can be null, can be reseated, needs *p to access and p->m for members; & takes an address, * dereferences

Comparison: use a reference when the argument is required and not null; use a pointer when it is optional (nullptr) or must be reseated; sizeof(pointer) is 8 bytes on 64-bit, a reference has no address of its own to use

Pass by value void f(T x) copies the argument, so the caller is unchanged; pass by reference void f(T& x) modifies the caller's object; pass by const reference void f(const T& x) avoids a copy and forbids modification, the default for large read-only parameters like std::string and std::vector

Mistake: returning a reference or pointer to a local variable is a dangling reference (UB); also a non-const T& cannot bind to a temporary, but const T& can; small types (int, double, char) are cheaper passed by value

chapters.title: Arrays, std::array and Pointer Decay
points: A C array int a[5] = {1,2,3}; has fixed size known at compile time, contiguous elements, and unspecified trailing elements zeroed only when an initializer list is given; no bounds checking, so a[5] is UB

Pointer decay: passing an array to a function turns it into int*, losing its size, so void f(int a[]) is really void f(int* a) and sizeof(a) inside gives the pointer size, not the array size; pass the length separately

std::array<int,5> a{1,2,3,4,5}; is a fixed-size zero-overhead wrapper: knows .size(), supports .at(i) with bounds checking (throws std::out_of_range), range-for, copy by assignment, and does not decay

Comparison: C array = fixed, decays, no .size(); std::array = fixed, stack, safe API; std::vector = resizable, heap storage, size set at runtime; prefer std::array when size is a compile-time constant
Mistake: sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) works only on a true array, not after decay; operator[] never checks bounds while .at() does; array size must be a compile-time constant, not a runtime variable

chapters.title: Stack vs Heap, new/delete and nullptr
points: Stack: automatic storage for locals, allocated and freed in LIFO order as scope ends, very fast, small (about 1 to 8 MB), so a huge local array or deep recursion causes stack overflow
Heap: dynamic storage via new/delete, lives until you free it, larger and slower, and may fragment; int* p = new int{5}; delete p; and arrays use new int[n] with delete[] p, never mixed

nullptr is the typed null pointer constant (type std::nullptr_t); prefer it over NULL or 0 because f(nullptr) picks the pointer overload while f(0) picks the int overload; deleting nullptr is safe, dereferencing it is UB
Prefer RAII over raw new/delete: std::make_unique<T>() frees automatically at scope end, std::vector replaces new[]; owning raw pointers are a code smell
Mistakes: memory leak (new without delete), double delete, use-after-free (p stays dangling, so set p = nullptr after delete), and mismatching new[] with delete

chapters.title: Function Overloading and the Header/Compilation Model
points: Overloading: same function name, different parameter lists (count or types); return type alone cannot distinguish overloads, and const-ness or reference on parameters can (f(int&) vs f(const int&))

Overload resolution ranks exact match, then promotion (char to int), then conversion (int to double), then user-defined conversion; an equally good match for two overloads is an ambiguity error, e.g. f(long) vs f(double) called with f(5)

Build pipeline: preprocessor (expands #include and #define) then compiler (each .cpp becomes one translation unit and an object file) then linker (resolves symbols across object files); g++ main.cpp util.cpp -o app

Headers hold declarations (prototypes, class definitions, templates, inline functions); .cpp files hold definitions; every header needs an include guard (#pragma once or #ifndef/#define/#endif) so repeated includes do not redefine things

Errors by phase: undefined reference is a linker error (declared but never defined, or the .cpp was not compiled in); multiple definition is a linker error from a non-inline function defined in a header, which violates the One Definition Rule; never put using namespace std; in a header

chapters.title: C++ Fundamentals Cheat Sheet
points: Types and init: prefer brace init {}, auto for obvious types, fixed-width ints from <cstdint>, constexpr for compile-time values, const everywhere possible; read const declarations right to left
Parameters: small types by value, large read-only by const T&, modify caller with T&, optional or nullable with T*; never return a reference or pointer to a local
Arrays: prefer std::array (fixed) or std::vector (resizable) over C arrays; use .at() when you want bounds checking; arrays decay to pointers when passed
Memory: stack is automatic and fast, heap needs new/delete (delete[] for new[]); prefer std::unique_ptr and make_unique; use nullptr, and set pointers to nullptr after delete

Build: declarations in .h with include guards, definitions in .cpp; preprocess, compile, link; undefined reference = missing definition, multiple definition = ODR violation; overloads differ by parameters, never by return type
